They produce a similar end result, a single commit containing the branch's changes, but they work on different things.

**`git merge --squash <branch>`** combines another branch into your current branch.

- It stages all of the other branch's changes as one set on your current branch.
- It does not commit. You run `git commit` yourself, writing one message.
- It records no merge relationship. The current branch gets no second parent, and Git doesn't know the commits were merged.
- The feature branch's commits stay as they were, so you can't later merge that branch cleanly with plain `git merge`. Git doesn't know its changes already landed, so it may try to reapply them and cause conflicts. `git branch -d` will also refuse to delete it, and you need `-D`.

**Interactive rebase squash** (`git rebase -i`, then marking commits `squash` or `fixup`) rewrites the commits on your own branch.

- It replaces several commits with one new commit, with a new SHA. The old commits disappear from the branch.
- It works on a single branch and doesn't involve merging anything.
- You can edit the combined message. `fixup` does the same thing but discards the absorbed commits' messages.
- If the branch was already pushed, you'll need to force-push, and anyone else who based work on those commits will have to reconcile.

**Typical use:**

- `merge --squash` is for integrating a feature branch into `main` as one commit when you don't want to rewrite the feature branch. Your feature branch remains as it was.
- `rebase -i` squash is for tidying your own commits before review or merge, such as folding "fix typo" commits into the commit they belong to. After that, a fast-forward or normal merge gives you a linear history.

If you're in a team workflow, a common combination is to clean up with `rebase -i` on the feature branch, then merge it into `main` with a plain fast-forward or merge commit. Or, if you want everything collapsed at merge time, use `merge --squash` and leave the feature branch's history alone.
